title: Psalm 120: A Song of Ascents Far from Home
summary: The psalmist, who has cried to the LORD and been answered, asks to be delivered from lying lips and a deceitful tongue, and warns the liar of God's arrows and burning coals. He laments living too long among people who hate peace, as though in distant Meshech and Kedar: he wants peace, but they want war.
story: Psalm 120 opens the Songs of Ascents, a collection of fifteen short psalms (120 to 134) that each carry the heading “A song of ascents.” Coming straight after the vast Psalm 119, these psalms follow a movement toward Jerusalem and the temple, ending with blessing in the house of the LORD in Psalm 134. Psalm 120 is the starting point, spoken from as far away as possible: from a place of lies and hostility, where the psalmist feels like an exile. The collection begins in distress and far from home, and each song draws nearer to Zion.
historical:
The meaning of the heading is debated. Many scholars think ascents refers to pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the three annual festivals, since the city sat in the hills and travelers always spoke of going up to it. The Mishnah (the collection of Jewish legal tradition compiled around AD 200) records a tradition that the Levites sang on fifteen steps leading up within the temple courts, corresponding to the fifteen Songs of Ascents. Others connect the title with the return from Babylon, which Ezra 7:9 calls a going up. Some also note that several of these psalms repeat a word from one line in the next, a stepping style that might explain the name. The views can overlap, and the pilgrimage reading is the most widely held.

Psalm 120 names no author, and its date is unknown. Several of the Songs of Ascents mention David or Solomon in their headings, but this one does not. Many scholars place the collection's final form after the exile, when Jews scattered across the Persian Empire made the trip to Jerusalem for festivals.
cultural:
Meshech was a people in the far north, in the region of Anatolia (modern Turkey), listed among the sons of Japheth in Genesis 10:2 and later named in Ezekiel 38:2 as a distant warlike nation. Kedar was an Arabian tribe of desert nomads living in black tents, descended from Ishmael according to Genesis 25:13 and known in Isaiah 21:16-17 for its archers. The two lay hundreds of miles apart, so the psalmist can hardly have lived in both. Most interpreters therefore read them as symbols: to live in Meshech and Kedar is to live among barbarous, hostile strangers at the ends of the known world.

The weapons of verse 4 fit the crime. A lying tongue was often compared to a sharp arrow or a sword in Israel's poetry (compare Psalm 64:3 and Jeremiah 9:8). The broom tree is a desert shrub whose roots and wood were used for fuel, and its coals burned hot. The punishment for the liar's piercing, burning words is God's own piercing arrows and burning coals.
literary: The psalm is a short individual lament in three parts. Verse 1 states that the psalmist cried and was answered, and verse 2 gives the content of his cry: deliverance from deceit. Verses 3 and 4 turn to address the deceitful tongue directly with a question and its answer, a common form in Israel's wisdom and curse language. Verses 5 to 7 are a lament over living among the hostile, built on the repeated word peace (shalom), which occurs in verses 6 and 7. The psalm ends not with resolution but with tension: the psalmist wants peace, and his neighbors want war. The rest of the Songs of Ascents supply the answer as they move toward Jerusalem, whose name many connected with peace.

outline.t: A cry for rescue from lying lips
What will the deceitful tongue receive?
Living among those who hate peace

doctrines.note: The psalm opens by remembering that God answered in the past, and that memory gives courage to pray again. The collection of pilgrim songs begins with a person who has no resource but crying to the LORD.

Lying and slander are not minor faults. The psalm pictures God answering the deceitful tongue with arrows and coals, which is to say that he takes the damage of false words seriously and will judge it.
The psalmist's longing for peace in a hostile place sets up the whole collection's movement toward Zion. Hope here is the ache for a home where peace is possible.

words.note: Shalom, peace, but far more than the absence of war. It means wholeness, well-being, and right relationships. The psalmist says literally that he is peace, while his neighbors hate it, and the word will return in the later Songs of Ascents in prayers for the peace of Jerusalem (Psalm 122).
Remiyyah, deceit or treachery. It describes the false tongue in verses 2 and 3. It names speech that looks reliable but betrays, the injury the psalmist has suffered.

Gur, to sojourn, to live as a resident foreigner without full rights or belonging. The psalmist says he sojourns in Meshech. The word carries the feeling of an outsider, someone who lives in a place without being at home there.

Meshech, a distant people of the far north. Named with Kedar in the far south and east, it stands for the most foreign and hostile places the psalmist can imagine. The geography is poetic, a way of saying he feels exiled among enemies.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 120, so the link is thematic. Jesus himself was surrounded by false witnesses at his trial (Mark 14:55-59), and he lived as one who wanted peace among those who wanted war, yet he did not answer lies with lies. He blessed peacemakers as children of God (Matthew 5:9), and Paul says Christ himself is our peace, breaking down hostility between peoples (Ephesians 2:14). The letter to the Hebrews describes believers as strangers and exiles on the earth seeking a homeland (Hebrews 11:13-16), which is the longing of a pilgrim who begins, like this psalm, far from the city of God.
questions: The psalmist feels like a foreigner among people who hate peace. Where do you feel most out of place because of your faith, and how do you respond?
The psalm treats lies as weapons. How have deceitful words wounded you, and how have your own words wounded others?
“I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war.” What does it look like to keep seeking peace when others refuse it?
